title: GitHub Collaboration, Pull Requests, and Actions CI/CD

segments.speaker: Lecturer
segments.text: GitHub hosts shared remote repositories under the default origin alias so distributed teams can coordinate changes without overwriting each other's local history. Cloning copies the full commit history locally, fetch downloads new remote commits safely without changing your working branch, pull fetches and integrates remote updates, and push publishes verified local commits back to GitHub.

segments.speaker: Lecturer
segments.text: Instead of committing unstable experiments directly onto main, developers isolate work inside short-lived feature branches and open a Pull Request before merging. A Pull Request compares the feature branch against main line by line, collects inline reviewer comments, and integrates changes using a merge commit to preserve branch history, squash merge to combine iterative commits into one clean entry, or rebase merge for a linear commit log.

segments.speaker: Lecturer
segments.topic_title: Code Review and Branch Protection Rules
segments.text: On main branches, repository maintainers enable branch protection rules so critical code cannot enter production unchecked. Protection enforces mandatory peer approvals, dismisses stale reviews automatically when new commits arrive, and blocks merging until required status checks pass, although maintainers must keep review scopes focused because oversized Pull Requests slow down thorough feedback.

segments.speaker: Lecturer
segments.text: GitHub Actions automates continuous integration and delivery using declarative YAML workflow files stored in the repository's .github/workflows directory. Events such as push or pull_request trigger parallel or sequential jobs on fresh virtual runners that build the project and run automated test suites, ensuring every Pull Request proves it compiles and passes checks before a reviewer approves the merge.
